title: “Everyone Knows One-and-Done PD Doesn’t Work”
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. pushes back on the common slogan that one-and-done professional development is useless. He offers three reasons: a large study of about 10,000 teachers found that effective PD is idiosyncratic and that neither job-embedded nor one-off formats are reliably better; his own career was launched by single workshops and keynotes, including Kelly Gallagher's and Ron Clark's; and the PD that has helped him took many forms with no shared format. He concedes that anecdotes prove nothing and that he has also sat through bad sessions. His conclusion is a caution against dogmatic sayings that flatten a complicated subject. The piece is a short but pointed argument for treating PD as varied and teacher-specific rather than ranking formats.
points: A study of roughly 10,000 teachers is cited to show that effective PD is idiosyncratic, so no single format can be declared worthless.
Stuart's own turning points, a Kelly Gallagher workshop and a Ron Clark keynote, were one-off events that shaped his career.
The PD that helped him most shared no format, ranging from books and writing institutes to being filmed and talking with colleagues.
The practical takeaway is to distrust slogans about PD and to judge a session by what it does for particular teachers.
quotes: One of the chief findings of a recent study on teacher professional development is that effective PD is pretty idiosyncratic. Basically, even the buzziest kinds of PD — “job-embedded,
differentiated,” — aren’t silver bullets (go figure), and the titularly maligned “one-and-done” types of PD (all-day workshops, keynotes) aren’t useless.

It was at a one-and-done, all-day Kelly Gallagher workshop in Grand Rapids when I started thinking, “Huh — that guy is a teacher who also writes and speaks about teaching. Maybe I could try doing that someday.” That was kind of a big thought for me — it eventually led to this moment in which I add the 302,000th word (or so; see Figure 1) to a blog that has made me the teacher I am today.

It was at a one-and-done, one hour keynote during my student teaching that I heard Ron Clark speak. While I only briefly adopted Clark’s eccentric The Essential 55 methods during the earliest part of my teaching career, the process of experimenting with Clark’s approach, as well as his energy and passion for teaching, were like rocket fuel at the start of my career.

My anecdotal evidence doesn’t prove my point, of course — and I’ve not shared with you the bad one-and-done PD experiences I’ve sat through as a teacher. But I don’t think I’m an outlier — many teachers I know have had their practice improved or their thinking clarified from one-and-done experiences.
I’m no different than any other teacher — I’ve had good and bad PD experiences. But the kinds of PD that have helped me in my work have only one thing in common: they’ve taken many forms.
We just need to be careful with dogmatic sayings like “Everyone knows one-and-done PD is bad.” That’s all I’m saying. Statements like that oversimplify a complex thing.
